questionText:
Read the following excerpt on K. Laxma Goud's 'Man, Woman and Tree' and answer the questions that follow:

Created in the 1970s using etching and aquatint on paper, 'Man, Woman and Tree' by K. Laxma Goud is an electrifying celebration of the raw, earthy vitality of rural India. Growing up in the agrarian village of Nizampur in Telangana and later training under K.G. Subramanyan at Baroda, Goud developed a graphic language steeped in tribal memory, peasant sexuality, and the symbiotic bond between human beings and nature. In 'Man, Woman and Tree', male and female figures are rendered with sharp, nervous, tactile lines, their limbs and bodies intimately intertwined with the twisting trunk and foliage of a sacred tree. Animals like goats and birds accompany the figures, visualising a world where human passion, animal instinct, and botanical growth share the same primal sap and cosmic fertility. Goud's incisive etching needle creates rich, dense textures of skin, hair, bark, and soil, capturing the uninhibited sensual pulse of the rural Deccan, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.

Question: In 'Man, Woman and Tree', how is the relationship between humanity and the tree portrayed?

questionText:
Read the following excerpt on Amrita Sher-Gil's 'Haldi Grinders' and answer the questions that follow:

Painted in 1940 at Saraya (Gorakhpur) using oil on canvas, 'Haldi Grinders' is one of the most poignant and celebrated mature masterpieces of Amrita Sher-Gil. Born to an Indian Sikh father and a Hungarian mother, Sher-Gil received elite academic training at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris before returning to India in 1934, declaring it her artistic destiny to interpret the life and silent melancholy of the Indian people. In 'Haldi Grinders', three rural women are depicted sitting upon the red earth under the shade of massive, curving tree trunks, grinding bright yellow turmeric using heavy stone pestles. Sher-Gil synthesizes European Post-Impressionism (Paul Gauguin) with the monumental dignity of Ajanta frescoes and the fiery color planes of Basohli miniatures. The glowing golden turmeric acts as an intense chromatic jewel against the deep terracotta red ground and dark tree trunks, capturing the silent endurance, tragic beauty, and timeless dignity of Indian village womanhood, conserved in the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), New Delhi.
